definition: The degree of ventricular myocardial stretch at the end of diastole, immediately before contraction. It is determined by the volume of blood in the ventricle at end-diastole and therefore by venous return.
formula: Approximated clinically by end-diastolic volume or pressure
typicalValue: LV end-diastolic volume ≈ 120 mL; LVEDP ≈ 4–12 mmHg

definition: The load the ventricle must overcome in order to eject blood. More precisely, it is ventricular wall stress during systole, which depends on chamber pressure, radius and wall thickness.
formula: Wall stress ≈ (P × r) ÷ (2 × wall thickness) — Laplace's law
typicalValue: Approximated by systemic vascular resistance or aortic systolic pressure

definition: The intrinsic ability of cardiac muscle to generate force at a given preload and afterload, independent of loading conditions.
formula: Best indexed by end-systolic elastance from pressure–volume loops

definition: The volume of blood ejected by a ventricle in a single contraction. It is determined by preload, afterload and contractility.
The volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute — the fundamental measure of the circulation's delivery capacity.
typicalValue: Approximately 5 L/min at rest; up to 20–25 L/min in trained athletes on maximal exercise

definition: The proportion of end-diastolic volume ejected with each beat. The single most used number in cardiology — but it is load-dependent and is not a pure measure of contractility.
The phase of ventricular contraction, comprising isovolumetric contraction and ejection. It begins with mitral and tricuspid closure (S1) and ends with aortic and pulmonary closure (S2).
typicalValue: Roughly one third of the cycle at rest; shortens relatively little as heart rate rises

definition: The phase of ventricular relaxation and filling, comprising isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, diastasis and atrial systole. Coronary perfusion of the left ventricle occurs almost entirely during diastole.
typicalValue: Roughly two thirds of the cycle at rest; shortens disproportionately with tachycardia

definition: The pressure gradient driving blood through the left coronary circulation during diastole.
formula: CPP = aortic diastolic pressure − left ventricular end-diastolic pressure

definition: The ratio of maximal hyperaemic coronary blood flow to resting flow — a measure of how much the coronary circulation can increase supply when demand rises.
The ratio of distal coronary pressure to aortic pressure during maximal hyperaemia, used to determine whether a stenosis is functionally significant.
formula: FFR = distal coronary pressure ÷ aortic pressure at maximal hyperaemia
typicalValue: Values at or below approximately 0.80 generally indicate a functionally significant lesion

definition: The total resistance to blood flow offered by the systemic circulation, residing predominantly in the arterioles.
formula: SVR = (MAP − right atrial pressure) ÷ cardiac output

definition: The average arterial pressure across a cardiac cycle — the pressure that actually drives organ perfusion.
formula: MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓ (systolic − diastolic); also MAP = CO × SVR

definition: The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure. It reflects stroke volume and large artery compliance, and widens as arteries stiffen with age.
The intrinsic property by which increasing end-diastolic fibre length increases the force of the subsequent contraction, so the heart automatically matches output to venous return.
The relationship between wall tension, pressure and radius. It explains why dilated ventricles work harder, why hypertrophy normalises wall stress, and why aneurysms enlarge at an accelerating rate.

The contribution of atrial contraction to ventricular filling in late diastole. It matters little at rest with a compliant ventricle, but becomes critical when the ventricle is stiff or the heart rate is fast.
Abnormal narrowing of a valve orifice or vessel lumen that obstructs flow. Across a stenotic valve, a pressure gradient develops that increases with flow.
Backward flow through a valve that fails to close completely, so part of the stroke volume returns to the upstream chamber and effective forward output falls.
Any abnormality of cardiac rate, rhythm, or the sequence of activation. Mechanisms are re-entry, enhanced automaticity and triggered activity.
The capacity of certain cardiac cells to depolarise spontaneously during phase 4 and reach threshold without external stimulation. The sinuatrial node has the fastest rate and therefore dominates.

A self-sustaining circuit in which an impulse repeatedly re-excites tissue that has recovered. It requires two pathways, unidirectional block and slow conduction, and accounts for most clinical tachyarrhythmias.
The pressure measured with a balloon-occluded pulmonary artery catheter, which approximates left atrial pressure and hence left ventricular filling pressure.
The pressure in the great veins near the right atrium, essentially equal to right atrial pressure. Estimated at the bedside from the jugular venous pressure.
Resistance to flow through the pulmonary circulation. Normally about one tenth of systemic vascular resistance, reflecting the low-pressure, high-compliance nature of the pulmonary bed.
formula: PVR = (mean PA pressure − PCWP) ÷ cardiac output

definition: An exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, caused by enhanced ventricular interdependence within a constrained pericardial space.
typicalValue: An inspiratory fall greater than 10 mmHg is abnormal

definition: A paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure during inspiration, occurring when the right heart cannot accommodate the increased venous return that inspiration normally produces.
The mechanical coupling of the two ventricles through the shared interventricular septum and the fixed pericardial space, so that filling of one influences filling of the other.
The elastic reservoir function of the aorta and large arteries, which stores energy during systole and releases it during diastole, converting pulsatile ejection into near-continuous peripheral flow.
The three categories of factor that predispose to thrombosis: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Nearly every risk factor for venous thromboembolism fits into one of them.
Increase in myocardial mass in response to load. Concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres in parallel) follows pressure overload; eccentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres in series) follows volume overload.

Progressive change in ventricular size, shape and composition following injury or chronic loading, involving myocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis and interstitial fibrosis. It is the structural pathway from injury to heart failure.
Inadequate blood supply relative to metabolic demand, producing reversible tissue dysfunction. Prolonged ischaemia leads to infarction — irreversible cell death.

A regulatory protein of the cardiac sarcomere released into the circulation when myocytes are injured. High-sensitivity assays detect very small elevations, so results must always be interpreted with the clinical context and a serial pattern.
typicalValue: Diagnostic threshold is the 99th percentile upper reference limit of a normal population

definition: Hormones released by cardiac myocytes in response to wall stretch. They promote natriuresis and vasodilatation, and their measurement is central to the diagnosis and risk stratification of heart failure.
typicalValue: Normal levels in an untreated symptomatic patient make heart failure very unlikely

definition: Uncoordinated contraction of ventricular segments caused by delayed electrical activation, most typically from left bundle branch block. It reduces pumping efficiency and is the target of cardiac resynchronisation therapy.
